That larger system includes the bodily shapes of the celestial spheres, their movements, the components of the physical and spiritual worlds, the relations between living bodies and the celestial spheres, and number itself.
That is the difference at the level of theory.

At the level of philosophical direction, the comparison leads us to another important conclusion. The difference is not only between the Brethren and the Pythagoreans. It also separates them from Platonism and Neoplatonism.
As we have seen from their own statements, the Brethren recognize that the material world really exists. In other words, they recognize its objective existence.

During this comparison, the Brethren of Purity’s idea of correspondence came clearly into view. Within that idea, we also encountered the role of numerical proportions and measurable quantities in the relations between things in the material world. The Brethren treat these proportions as one form of correspondence—or as one expression of the overall order they believe governs existence.

Their idea of correspondence reminds us of the idea of harmony that dominates Plotinus’s view of the world. In his case, harmony served as an ideological expression of his “justification” of the slave system.
Does this mean that the Brethren’s correspondence and Plotinus’s harmony are really the same thing?

Of course, we cannot say that the Brethren learned nothing from Plotinus’s idea of harmony. On the contrary, they were probably influenced by it. But the two ideas begin from different philosophical and ideological positions.
For Plotinus, harmony begins from a determinist outlook dominated by a sense that fate rules everything. This reflects the ideology of the slave-based social order expressed in his philosophy.
In the Brethren’s idea of correspondence, by contrast, human will and choice become part of the picture wherever human activity is involved.

This too is connected with their ideology. Their ideas express social and class interests and ambitions that conflict with the principle of absolute necessity, or determinism. That principle lay at the heart of the ideology of the ruling caliphate, which presented its authority as something required by divine necessity—by God’s decree and predestination.
The role of will and choice appears in several areas of the Brethren’s thought.

We see it first in the way they present correspondence itself. When they discuss how conflicting things come together and form a unified whole, they do not say that this happens through an unavoidable necessity.
We may recall their statement in an earlier passage that hostile and conflicting elements “cannot come together unless someone brings them together.”
And this “someone who brings them together” is not a will that exists outside the world. Their own practical examples make that clear.

All of the examples involve deliberate human action. A musician takes clashing notes and turns them into a unified musical pattern. A painter brings contrasting colors together into a harmonious whole. A chemist combines different substances in measured proportions and produces a new substance in which those differences are united. A cook takes different ingredients, tastes, colors, and smells and combines them into a single dish in which the differences work together.
In every one of these examples, the combination is clearly produced through the will of the person doing the combining.
9 — A Turn Toward Quantitative Rather Than Qualitative Analysis
There is something very important here that deserves our attention: the Brethren’s idea of numerical proportions and measurable quantities, and the effects these have on the way things change.
This idea points to a clear development among the scientists of their age. They were increasingly studying natural and social phenomena through experiment and through quantitative analysis.
In this respect, they moved beyond the tendency of ancient philosophy and science—that is, the metaphysical approach that stopped at the fixed and static qualities of things and essences.
This move toward quantity was an important historical step toward explaining qualitative changes in the movement of matter through quantitative changes.

These scientists and philosophers understood that quantitative proportions could produce new quantities of matter. At the same time, they had a relative understanding of the dialectic of opposing forces and of the way opposites can form a unity.

Together, these ideas represented an advanced step for their age in the development of scientific and practical thought. They also marked progress in attempts to explain the world by understanding the movement of matter.

This point confirms something we argued earlier. The encyclopedic character of the Brethren’s work was a feature of an entire historical age. It was not simply the product of a limited Shiʿi or Ismāʿīlī sectarian movement confined within the boundaries of religious thought, as most Orientalists and many modern Arab researchers have claimed.
10 — One Way of Understanding Necessity and Freedom

Let us return to the role of free will and choice in the Brethren’s system of correspondence. Another passage gives us what was, in relative terms, an advanced way of understanding necessity and freedom—perhaps even by the standards of their own age.
The passage appears in their discussion of the benefits of astrology:

“Know, my brother, that there are many benefits in knowing the science of the stars. One is that if a person knows that some event will happen in the future, or after a number of days, he may be able to protect himself from some of its effects—not by preventing it from happening, but by guarding against it or preparing for it. This is what people normally do. They prepare for the cold of winter by gathering warm coverings, and for the heat of summer by seeking shelter. They prepare for years of high prices by storing supplies, flee from places of unrest and keep their distance from them, and avoid travel when there is danger...”

Even if we do not remove from their argument their belief in a regular causal connection between the movements of the stars and events on Earth, especially events in human life, and even if we do not remove the supernatural methods they mention in this context for protecting people from the harmful effects of natural laws, the words quoted above still have a clear significance.

They show that the Brethren had some awareness of the relation between necessity and freedom, even though they did not know how to formulate the issue in the terms later used by the laws of dialectical materialism.

Their meaning is quite clear. They understood that necessity—to use our modern term—is not an unavoidable fate from which there is no escape. If human beings learn its laws—notice their words, “Know, my brother, that there are many benefits in knowing the science of the stars”—that is, if they learn the laws of nature, they can free themselves from some of their harmful effects.
We do not have the right to go a step further and add that human beings can make those laws serve their own interests.
First, the Brethren themselves did not say this. Second, the historical conditions in which they lived were not yet developed enough for the idea to be expressed in this form.

To sum up, the place given to number and to numerical and measurable proportions in the Brethren’s philosophy represents one form of correspondence, which they see as a general system and not as something limited to number alone.

Second, their treatment of these proportions represents a progressive intellectual position on the relations between things in the material world—a world whose real, concrete, objective existence they recognize.

The importance of this progressive element is not limited to the theoretical advances made in the natural sciences, including mathematics, among the Arabs of the Brethren’s age. It also points to progress in linking theoretical thought with experiment in these sciences.

Our purpose in the comparisons made in this section has been to make clear the basic difference—in philosophical direction and ideological content—between the philosophy of the Brethren of Purity on the one hand, and Pythagoreanism, Platonism, and Neoplatonism on the other.
The difference is this: those three philosophies deny the material world an objective existence, while the Brethren’s philosophy recognizes that the material world exists objectively.
Their philosophy also contains materialist positions in several areas. But these positions do not remove it from its overall idealist framework.
As we continue our discussion of the Brethren’s philosophy, we may encounter further evidence supporting this argument.
11 — Early Seeds of a Theory of Natural Evolution
We have now seen several things about the Brethren of Purity’s view of nature.

They looked toward quantitative changes as a basis for qualitative changes in nature. They treated causal relations between things in the natural world as a basic condition of knowledge. They rejected miracles, supernatural events, and knowledge of the unseen even for prophets and messengers. In some of their texts, they even rejected a supernatural basis for revelation, inspiration, and astrological prediction. And they treated the external, material world as something that really and objectively exists.

Once we have seen all this, it becomes easier to understand how their picture of natural formation could contain an early, embryonic seed of a theory of the evolution of species—a theory that did not enter the language of science until the middle of the nineteenth century.
Perhaps this step followed from the others. Perhaps it helped produce them. Perhaps the developments simply occurred alongside one another.
That is not the important question here.

What matters is that all these elements appear together. Taken as a whole, they show that the Brethren’s encyclopedic work, produced during the great scientific age of Arab civilization in the fourth Islamic century—the tenth century CE—recorded one of the major features of that age: a growing tendency to explain the world in materialist terms, driven underneath by ideological forces.
This was no doubt connected with the growing and deepening interaction between knowledge of nature and society on the one hand, and the production of material necessities on the other.
At the same time, class divisions were becoming sharper and productive forces were breaking through older limits within this society.

Taken together, these conditions inevitably found an expression in the world of ideas. Ideological conflicts developed between thinkers who came from peasant, artisan, or impoverished social groups and the state, which served as the political power of the economically dominant class.
These thinkers also needed weapons for their ideological confrontation with the state. The new scientific knowledge itself became one of those weapons.

So if our impression is correct that the Brethren had, in some form, arrived at an idea of the evolution of species, this would mean that they had raised against the official ideology the sharpest weapon known to the ideological conflicts of their age.
But we cannot accept that impression without qualification.
The problem is that we have a number of texts preserved in their encyclopedia, the Epistles, and these texts have a meaning and content that we cannot simply ignore.
So let us read them carefully, while keeping our reservations in mind, and then ask what they are actually saying.
The first passage is directed against the theologians who claimed that God was the direct source of the actions of nature.
The Brethren write that these theologians:

“Because they did not know what nature is, attributed all its actions to the Creator (...) and fell into great confusion, bewilderment, and doubt. They understood that every action must have an agent, and when they saw actions whose agent they could not see, they attributed them to the Creator (...) Then they examined these actions and found that some of them were evil and destructive, such as the deaths of children, the misfortunes of good people, the power given to the wicked, the destruction of animals and the injuries, pains, ignorance, and afflictions that befall them (...) We have already explained that all these are the actions of individual souls, all of which are powers of the universal celestial soul as its Creator brought it into being (...) Whatever is good among these actions is attributed to the good individual soul, and whatever is evil is attributed to the evil soul, which then receives its due reward or punishment. Know, my brother, that your soul is one of these individual souls. It is one power among the powers of the universal soul. It is not identical with the universal soul, nor is it separate from it, just as your body is one part of the body of the world: it is not the whole world, but neither is it separate from it...”
What do we learn from this passage?
The direct cause of the actions of nature and of human beings is nature itself and the human being himself. The “individual soul” is the individual being—the particular thing or person.
We know this because elsewhere in the Epistles the Brethren say that the human being consists of the soul and the body together, “the combination of the two.”

Their statement that “the individual soul is one power among the powers of the universal celestial soul” reflects another part of their view: the celestial world and the earthly world are connected by life, by corporeality—that is, material existence—and by movement, the continuous and unbroken movement of change.
At the same time, each of these two worlds has an existence of its own.

This is what they mean when they say that the individual soul is not identical with the universal soul, but is not separate from it either, just as your body is part of the body of the world without being the whole world or being separated from it.
That concerns the actions carried out by nature and human beings.
But what about the original formation of nature, including the formation of the human being?
After explaining how the world of the celestial spheres and the world of the four elements are formed from absolute body, the Brethren write:
“Then the spheres revolve around the elements, causing them to mix with one another. From them emerge the generated beings: minerals, plants, and animals.”
Now consider this passage alongside another:

“Universal matter—that is, absolute body—passed through a long period of time before it went through a process of formation and its subtle part became separated from its dense part; before it received the different spherical forms of the heavens, arranged one inside another; before the bodies of the luminous stars became round and took their positions; and before the four elements became distinct, took their proper places, and entered into their ordered system.”

From these two passages, we can understand the celestial bodies, the elements of nature, and the minerals, plants, and animals that arose from them as having formed through an internal process that unfolded in stages.

The process began with absolute body. It took a long period of time before this body entered a new stage of formation. During that stage, a kind of “selection” took place: the subtle became separated from the dense.
This “selection” then allowed absolute body to take on its first material forms—the spherical forms of the celestial spheres.
The process then continued within these forms, with the spheres being “arranged one inside another.”
From there it passed into another stage, until “the bodies of the luminous stars became round” and “took their positions.”
At this point, another kind of selection took place. The four elements became distinct from one another, meaning that each acquired its own particular natural qualities.
Once those qualities appeared, the process continued by arranging the elements in their different levels and ordering the laws of their movement.
We find the answer in another passage.
In summary, the Brethren say that after the elements “mixed with one another,” they produced the “generated beings”: minerals, plants, and animals.
They describe the way these beings emerged in a kind of ascending sequence, from lower forms to higher ones.
Minerals appeared first. Plants came next, followed by animals.

Their explanation is that the lower form serves as a tool and material for the one that comes after it. Minerals provide the material for the formation of plants, while minerals and plants together provide the material for the formation of animals.
Animal life itself then develops from lower to higher forms until it reaches the human being.
The human being is therefore the highest of the generated beings found on Earth.

Why, then, does the world of the simple substances begin with the highest and move downward—the active intellect, then the universal soul, then prime matter, then nature—while the physical world moves in the opposite direction, from lower forms to higher ones?

The Brethren answer that the luminous substances contain no composition, difference, or variation of the kind found in physical things. Their only differences come from their rank and from how close they are to God.
The physical world, by contrast, is subject to decay and transformation. It therefore begins with what is lower and ends with what is better.
That is why human beings appeared only after minerals, plants, and animals already existed. Human beings need and benefit from all three.
If human beings had appeared before them, the Brethren say, their creation would have been pointless, because they could not survive or live without them.
This gives us a picture in which earthly beings are “generated” through an ascending sequence.
The lower form is “a tool used by what comes after it,” while animal life itself develops through different forms, rising from lower forms to higher ones until the human being appears.

Of course, the Brethren themselves do not use the words “evolution,” “selection,” “process,” or “species” in any of these passages. These words are our way of translating the picture they present in the language of their own age.
But the picture itself is not far from what those terms describe.
The idea of a process, which is the key point here, is especially close to being stated directly in their texts, even if they use different words.
And there are other passages that strengthen this impression.

One says that minerals, plants, and animals can transform into one another as their qualities change, as their quantities differ, as their structures vary, and as those structures change into one another.
